Where, when, and why TTC delays concentrate

A stakeholder briefing for TTC service planning

Lionael Surya

2026-11-14

Headline

Reported TTC delay is overwhelmingly a bus problem, and serious delays are worst overnight. Bus accounts for 64.8% of the 1,251,597 reported incidents and 83.9% of all reported delay minutes in the extract. The share of incidents lasting 15 minutes or more is 25.7% overall, and the early-morning hours have the highest severity rate on bus and streetcar. This is a descriptive and predictive analysis, not a causal one.

What the data cover

The extract runs from 2014-01-01 to 2026-09-30 and contains 1,251,597 incidents across subway, bus, and streetcar. The pipeline downloads the City of Toronto’s yearly files and the rolling since-2025 extract, harmonises two legacy schemas and one newer schema, and loads the result into PostgreSQL. Full method notes are in docs/STATISTICAL_METHODS.md; limitations are in docs/LIMITATIONS.md.

Three pictures

1. Daily volume: the pandemic, then a partial recovery

28-day rolling average of reported incidents per day, by mode.

The shaded COVID period is visible in all three modes. Daily counts recovered after 2022, but the series still shows the reporting disruption around the pandemic. The last point may reflect a partial month in the rolling extract.

2. Major delays concentrate overnight

Share of incidents lasting 15 minutes or more, by weekday and hour.

The heatmap is the clearest operational result. Bus and streetcar severity is highest between roughly midnight and 05:00, not during the afternoon peak. The logistic model agrees: hour 3 has an odds ratio of 1.71 relative to midnight, while the PM peak is lower than midnight. Subway severity stays low throughout the day.

3. Delay minutes sit on a small set of streetcar lines, not on a small set of bus lines

Top lines by reported delay minutes.

The top 10 bus lines account for 17.4% of bus delay minutes. The top 5 streetcar lines account for 74.0%. YU and BD together account for 89.6% of subway delay minutes. A network-wide bus fix is therefore a different problem from a line-specific streetcar fix.

What predicts a major delay

The pre-registered logistic model (15-minute outcome, trained 2014-2023, scored on 2024) reaches an AUC of 0.756 (95% CI 0.753 to 0.759). That is useful but not precise. On the 2024 holdout the mean predicted probability is 24.2% against an observed rate of 28.1%, so the model under-predicts severity in that year.

Plant/infrastructure causes have higher odds of a major delay than equipment (odds ratio 2.17). Subway has much lower odds than bus (0.046). The count model finds lower daily incident counts during COVID (rate ratio 0.79) and on weekends. The year term is 1.005.

Three recommendations for service planners

  1. Treat overnight recovery as a distinct operating problem. The severity peak is between midnight and 05:00 on bus and streetcar. That points to recovery time, access to vehicles and staff, and terminal conditions, not just afternoon congestion.
  2. Separate the bus and streetcar strategies. Bus delay is spread across many lines, so line-by-line targeting will miss most of it. Streetcar delay is concentrated: 501, 504, 506, 505, and 510 carry most of the streetcar delay minutes.
  3. Fix the measurement before using delay minutes as a KPI. Legacy bus and streetcar files use coarse cause labels, and 1,233 records contain a 999-minute placeholder. Changing the codebook and removing sentinel values would make year-over-year comparisons more trustworthy.

Limitations

The data are observational and contain no ridership, weather, construction, or staffing. Cause categories are coarse before 2021. The final month of the rolling extract may be partial. The 2024 holdout is one year and is harder than the training period. All results are associations, not causal effects. The full list is in docs/LIMITATIONS.md.

Data and reproducibility

Data: City of Toronto Open Data, TTC Subway, Bus, and Streetcar Delay Data, Open Government Licence - Toronto. Code: ttc-delay-analysis, MIT licensed. The pipeline is Rscript scripts/run_all.R or make pipeline. Generated tables and figures are in outputs/; the complete findings are in docs/FINDINGS.md.
